passages.title: Volunteer Network Captures Rare Flash on the Moon's Dark Side
paragraphs: A loose network of amateur astronomers, coordinated by a small regional observatory in northern Thailand, has recorded what researchers believe is the brightest lunar impact flash yet documented in mainland Southeast Asia. The flash, which lasted roughly a third of a second, was captured on the evening of 14 August by three volunteers working independently in Chiang Rai, Nan and Luang Prabang.

Impact flashes occur when meteoroids strike the lunar surface at speeds that can exceed 20 kilometres per second. Because the Moon has no atmosphere to slow incoming debris, even small fragments release enough energy to produce a brief burst of light. Such events can only be observed on the unlit portion of the Moon, where the flash is not drowned out by reflected sunlight, and they are so fleeting that a single sighting is generally treated with caution.

It was precisely this problem that the network was set up to address. According to Dr. Kanokwan Siripat, an astronomer at the Mae Kok Observatory, a flash recorded by only one camera could easily be a cosmic ray striking the sensor, a satellite briefly reflecting the sun, or simply electronic noise. “A single video is an anecdote,” she said. “Two or more, taken hundreds of kilometres apart, become evidence.” Because the three recordings agree on both the timing and the position of the flash, the team is confident that the event was genuine.

Preliminary estimates suggest that the object weighed between 3 and 6 kilograms and left a crater perhaps 8 to 12 metres across. The researchers stress, however, that these figures rest on assumptions about the impactor's speed and about how efficiently its energy was converted into visible light, neither of which can be measured directly. They have therefore shared their data with scientists working on a lunar orbiter, in the hope that the spacecraft can photograph the site and confirm whether a fresh crater exists.

Beyond its scientific value, the observation has been welcomed as a vindication of citizen science. The network's members use modest telescopes and inexpensive video cameras, many of them bought second-hand, and most have no formal training in astronomy. Their work is nonetheless attracting growing interest from engineers: as several countries plan crewed missions and permanent bases on the Moon, a clearer picture of how often the surface is struck could inform the design of shielding for equipment and habitats.

Not everyone expects rapid progress. Dr. Somchai Phanthong, a planetary scientist who was not involved in the project, cautioned that a handful of recorded flashes cannot yet yield a reliable impact rate. “We need years of systematic monitoring, not a few lucky nights,” he said. The network appears to agree; it plans to recruit a further twenty observers across the Mekong region by the end of next year.

questions.q: What is the main idea of the passage?
options: Amateur astronomers have shown that professional observatories are no longer needed to study the Moon.
A lunar impact flash confirmed by several volunteers has been welcomed, though its wider significance is still limited.
Engineers have begun designing lunar bases using data collected by a network of volunteers.
A meteoroid weighing several kilograms has been proved to have left a new crater on the Moon.
questions.explain: บทความรายงานว่าเครือข่ายอาสาสมัครบันทึกแสงวาบได้พร้อมกันหลายจุด (¶1, ¶3) และได้รับการยกย่อง (¶5) แต่ ¶6 เตือนว่า “a handful of recorded flashes cannot yet yield a reliable impact rate” จึงตอบ B ตัวเลือก D ล่อใจเพราะมีตัวเลขน้ำหนักจาก ¶4 แต่บทความบอกว่าเป็นเพียงการประมาณ และยังรอยานโคจร “confirm whether a fresh crater exists” จึงยังไม่ได้ 'พิสูจน์'

questions.q: It can be inferred from paragraph 2 that impact flashes on the sunlit part of the Moon
options: are rarer because fewer meteoroids strike that side
release less energy than those on the unlit side
are slowed down by a thin layer of lunar gases
probably occur but cannot be seen against the bright, sunlit surface
questions.explain: ¶2: flashes “can only be observed on the unlit portion of the Moon, where the flash is not drowned out by reflected sunlight” แสดงว่าด้านที่มีแสงก็น่าจะเกิดแสงวาบเช่นกัน เพียงแต่มองไม่เห็นเพราะแสงอาทิตย์กลบ จึงตอบ D ตัวเลือก A ล่อใจแต่บทความไม่ได้บอกว่าอุกกาบาตตกด้านใดมากกว่า ส่วน C ขัดกับ “the Moon has no atmosphere”

questions.q: Why does Dr. Kanokwan say that “A single video is an anecdote” in paragraph 3?
options: To explain why sightings from several separate locations were essential
To criticise volunteers who share their videos before checking them
To suggest that video cameras are less reliable than telescopes
To admit that the August flash may not have been a real event

questions.q: In paragraph 4, the phrase 'these figures' refers to
options: the impact speeds of over 20 kilometres per second given in paragraph 2
the times at which the three volunteers recorded the flash
the estimated mass of the object and the size of its crater
the images that the lunar orbiter is expected to provide

questions.q: Which of the following best expresses the meaning of the second sentence of paragraph 4?
options: The estimates depend on two factors that the team was unable to observe.
The team measured the object's speed but not the light it produced.
The researchers doubt that the object struck the Moon at all.
The figures were calculated from direct measurements of the crater.

questions.q: The word 'vindication' in paragraph 5 is closest in meaning to
options: a fresh challenge to
evidence of the value of
an official reward for
a defence against complaints about

questions.q: According to paragraph 5, why are engineers increasingly interested in the network's work?
options: Cheap second-hand cameras could replace costly instruments on future missions.
The volunteers could train engineers to monitor the Moon at night.
Impact flashes might provide a source of light for future lunar bases.
Knowing how often the Moon is hit could help protect future structures there.
questions.explain: ¶5: “a clearer picture of how often the surface is struck could inform the design of shielding for equipment and habitats” จึงตอบ D ตัวเลือก A ล่อใจเพราะใช้คำ “second-hand” และ “inexpensive” จากย่อหน้าเดียวกัน แต่นั่นเป็นคำบรรยายอุปกรณ์ของอาสาสมัคร ไม่ใช่เหตุผลที่วิศวกรสนใจ

questions.q: Dr. Somchai's attitude towards the network's findings can best be described as
options: dismissive, since he doubts that the flash was genuine
enthusiastic, since the findings settle the question of impact rates
cautious about how much they can reveal at this stage
indifferent, because he took no part in the project

passages.title: Notice to Members: Revised Outpatient Benefits and Pre-Approval Rules
paragraphs: Members of the Northeastern Universities Staff Health Scheme are advised that, following the annual review of the scheme by its governing board, a number of changes to benefits and procedures will take effect for all policies renewed on or after 1 April 2027. Members whose policies renew before that date will continue under the current terms until their next renewal. Nothing in this notice affects claims for treatment that has already been received.

The most significant change concerns outpatient care. At present, members may claim up to 1,500 baht per visit with no annual ceiling. From the renewal date, the per-visit limit will rise to 2,000 baht, but total outpatient claims will be capped at 30,000 baht per member per policy year. The board recognises that this ceiling will affect some members who visit clinics frequently. However, the scheme's actuarial review found that fewer than 4 per cent of members exceeded this amount in the past three years, whereas rising claim costs, if left unchecked, would have required an across-the-board increase in contributions of roughly 11 per cent.

Members with long-term conditions such as diabetes, hypertension or chronic kidney disease, who may be disproportionately affected by the ceiling, are encouraged to enrol in the scheme's Chronic Care Pathway. Enrolled members receive medication and routine monitoring through designated partner clinics, and these costs are not counted towards the outpatient ceiling. Enrolment requires a referral from a registered physician and may be completed at any time during the policy year.

Second, the list of procedures requiring pre-approval will be extended. In addition to non-emergency surgery, members must now obtain written approval before undergoing MRI or CT scans, and before any inpatient admission planned more than 48 hours in advance. Requests should be submitted through the member portal at least five working days beforehand. Claims for listed procedures carried out without approval may be reduced by up to 50 per cent, except where the treating doctor certifies that the delay required to obtain approval would have endangered the patient's health.
Third, the waiting period for dental and optical benefits for new members will be shortened from twelve months to six. Existing members are unaffected by this change.

Contribution rates for the coming year will remain unchanged for all age bands. The board wishes to stress that this outcome was made possible largely by the introduction of the outpatient ceiling described above.

Members who wish to comment on these changes may do so in writing to the Scheme Secretariat until 28 February 2027. Comments received will be considered at the board's next meeting, although the board does not undertake to respond to individual submissions. A full schedule of benefits is available on the member portal or from the human resources office of each participating university.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of this notice?
options: To persuade members to renew their policies before 1 April 2027
To announce that members' contributions will rise in the coming year
To inform members of revised benefits and rules and when they apply
To invite members to vote on changes that the board has proposed

questions.q: What can be inferred from paragraph 1 about a member whose policy renews on 1 January 2027?
options: The member will keep the current benefits until the policy renews again.
The member will be moved to the new terms on 1 April 2027.
The member will lose cover for treatment already received.
The member will have to apply again in order to stay in the scheme.
questions.explain: ¶1: “Members whose policies renew before that date will continue under the current terms until their next renewal” ผู้ที่ต่ออายุวันที่ 1 มกราคม 2027 (ก่อน 1 เมษายน) จึงใช้เงื่อนไขเดิมไปจนถึงการต่ออายุครั้งถัดไป ตอบ A ตัวเลือก B ล่อใจเพราะใช้วันที่ 1 April แต่วันนั้นใช้กับกรมธรรม์ที่ต่ออายุ 'ในหรือหลัง' วันดังกล่าวเท่านั้น

questions.q: Which of the following best summarises the change to the outpatient benefit?
options: A lower payment for each visit, but no limit on the total for the year
A yearly limit of 2,000 baht that replaces the limit for each visit
An increase of about 11 per cent in the amount paid for each visit
A larger payment for each visit, combined with a new limit on the yearly total

questions.q: Why does the notice mention the figure of 11 per cent in paragraph 2?
options: To report how much claim costs rose over the past three years
To show the cost of an alternative that the board wished to avoid
To indicate the proportion of members who will reach the ceiling
To announce the new contribution rate for all age bands
questions.explain: ¶2: rising costs “if left unchecked, would have required an across-the-board increase in contributions of roughly 11 per cent” ตัวเลขนี้ใช้แสดงผลของทางเลือกอื่นที่คณะกรรมการไม่ต้องการ เพื่อสนับสนุนการกำหนดเพดาน ตอบ B ตัวเลือก D ล่อใจแต่ ¶6 ระบุว่าเงินสมทบไม่เปลี่ยน และ C สับสนกับตัวเลข “fewer than 4 per cent”

options: can enrol only at the beginning of a policy year
is less likely to reach the outpatient ceiling
no longer needs a doctor's referral for treatment

questions.q: Under the new rules, which of the following does NOT require pre-approval?
options: an inpatient admission arranged at short notice in an emergency
a CT scan recommended by the member's doctor
surgery that is not needed as an emergency

questions.q: According to paragraph 4, a claim for an MRI scan carried out without approval may still be paid in full if
options: the member submits a request within five working days afterwards
the scan was planned more than 48 hours before it took place
the treating doctor confirms that waiting would have put the patient at risk
the member has already paid the full cost of the scan

questions.q: In paragraph 7, the phrase 'does not undertake to respond' is closest in meaning to
options: does not attempt to respond
is not able to respond
has not yet begun to respond
does not promise to respond

passages.title: Four Easy Payments: The Hidden Cost of Buying Now and Paying Later
paragraphs: When Pimchanok, a 26-year-old graphic designer in Bangkok, bought a 12,000-baht phone last year, she did not use a credit card. Instead, she tapped a button at the online checkout that split the price into four interest-free instalments. Within six months, she had seven such plans running at once. “Each one felt tiny,” she recalls. “It was only when I listed them all that I realised a third of my salary was spoken for before it arrived.”

Pimchanok's experience is hardly unusual. Buy-now-pay-later (BNPL) services, which allow shoppers to spread the cost of a purchase over several weeks or months, have expanded rapidly across Southeast Asia, particularly among consumers under thirty. Unlike credit cards, they rarely involve a lengthy application, and the providers, which earn most of their revenue from fees charged to retailers rather than to shoppers, present themselves as a fairer alternative to traditional lending.

Yet a growing body of research suggests that the convenience comes at a cost that is less visible than an interest rate. A 2025 survey of 2,400 BNPL users by researchers in central Thailand found that 38 per cent had missed at least one payment in the previous year, and that those holding three or more plans simultaneously were twice as likely to report difficulty paying household bills. Late fees, while modest individually, accumulated quickly for these users.

Behavioural economists offer an explanation. When a price is broken into smaller parts, they argue, people tend to judge each part in isolation, a tendency sometimes called “payment partitioning”. A purchase of 3,000 baht feels markedly cheaper when presented as four payments of 750, even though the total is identical. Retailers appear well aware of this effect: several have reported that shoppers who choose BNPL spend on average 20 to 30 per cent more per order.

Industry representatives dispute the more alarming interpretations. They point out that most users repay on time, that missed BNPL payments typically involve far smaller sums than credit card debt, and that many customers use the service deliberately to manage their cash flow between paydays. Even some consumer advocates concede that, for disciplined users, the product can be cheaper than a credit card.

The central difficulty, critics say, is that the product is largely invisible to the wider financial system. Because many BNPL providers do not report to credit bureaus, a bank assessing a loan application may have no idea that the applicant is already committed to a dozen instalment plans. Regulators in several countries are now considering rules that would oblige providers to check affordability and share repayment data with credit bureaus. Providers warn that such measures would add friction to a service whose chief selling point is simplicity.

For her part, Pimchanok has deleted the apps from her phone. “I'm not saying they're evil,” she says. “But nobody tells you that the hard part isn't paying for one thing. It's keeping track of all of them.”

questions.q: What is the main idea of the passage?
options: Instalment services are convenient but may lead some users into debt that is hard to keep track of.
Instalment services should be banned because they charge high rates of interest to young people.
Most young people in Southeast Asia now prefer instalment services to credit cards.
Retailers have been forced to lower their prices because of the spread of instalment services.
questions.explain: บทความชี้ว่า BNPL สะดวก (¶2) แต่ “the convenience comes at a cost that is less visible than an interest rate” (¶3) และปัญหาคือการติดตามหนี้หลายก้อน (¶6–¶7) จึงตอบ A ตัวเลือก B ผิดเพราะบริการนี้เป็นแบบ “interest-free” และบทความไม่ได้เสนอให้ห้าม ส่วน C สรุปเกินจากที่บทความบอกเพียงว่าขยายตัว “particularly among consumers under thirty”

questions.q: Why does the writer begin the article with Pimchanok's story?
options: To show that graphic designers earn too little to buy expensive phones
To argue that young people should never use online shopping services
To illustrate through a personal case how small commitments can build up
To prove that most users of the service have more than seven plans
questions.explain: ¶1 เล่าว่าแต่ละรายการ “felt tiny” แต่เมื่อรวมกันแล้ว “a third of my salary was spoken for” และ ¶2 กล่าวต่อว่า “Pimchanok's experience is hardly unusual” เรื่องเล่านี้จึงใช้ยกตัวอย่างว่าภาระเล็กๆ สะสมกันได้ ตอบ C ตัวเลือก D สรุปเกินจริงจากกรณีเดียว (overgeneralisation)

questions.q: According to paragraph 2, BNPL providers earn most of their income from
options: interest charged on late repayments
charges paid by the shops that offer the service
application fees paid by new customers
selling their customers' data to banks
questions.explain: ¶2: providers “earn most of their revenue from fees charged to retailers rather than to shoppers” คือรายได้หลักมาจากร้านค้า ตอบ B ตัวเลือก A ล่อใจเพราะ ¶3 กล่าวถึง late fees แต่ไม่ได้บอกว่าเป็นรายได้หลัก และ C ขัดกับข้อความว่าบริการนี้ “rarely involve a lengthy application”

questions.q: What can be inferred from the survey described in paragraph 3?
options: Most BNPL users are unable to pay their household bills.
Late fees are the main reason people sign up for several plans.
Users with only one plan never miss a payment.
Holding several plans at once appears to be linked to wider money problems.
questions.explain: ¶3: ผู้ที่มี “three or more plans simultaneously were twice as likely to report difficulty paying household bills” แสดงความเชื่อมโยงระหว่างการมีหลายแผนกับปัญหาการเงินอื่น ตอบ D ตัวเลือก A ใช้คำว่า Most ซึ่งเกินจากข้อมูล (38 per cent เป็นเรื่องการผิดนัดชำระ ไม่ใช่ค่าบ้าน) ส่วน C ไม่มีข้อมูลรองรับ

questions.q: In paragraph 4, the phrase 'people tend to judge each part in isolation' means that people
options: consider each payment separately rather than thinking about the total
prefer to make their purchases alone rather than with friends
compare the prices of different products before buying
find it hard to calculate the total cost of large purchases
questions.explain: ¶4: เมื่อราคาถูกแบ่งเป็นส่วน คนจะพิจารณาแต่ละส่วนแยกกัน ตัวอย่างคือ 3,000 บาท “feels markedly cheaper when presented as four payments of 750, even though the total is identical” ตอบ A ตัวเลือก B ล่อใจเพราะเล่นกับความหมายตรงของ isolation (โดดเดี่ยว) ซึ่งไม่ตรงกับบริบท

questions.q: What does the writer suggest about retailers in paragraph 4?
options: They are worried that BNPL is harming their customers.
They charge higher prices to customers who choose BNPL.

passages.title: The Greenest Building Is Often the One Already Standing
paragraphs: Every few months, another row of old shophouses in one of our provincial cities disappears behind hoarding, and a year or two later a glass-fronted tower rises in its place, accompanied by a press release celebrating its energy-efficient lighting and rooftop solar panels. We are invited to see this as progress. It is time we questioned that assumption.

The case for new construction usually rests on operating energy: the electricity a building consumes for cooling, lighting and equipment over its lifetime. On this measure, modern buildings undoubtedly outperform most older ones. What the press releases rarely mention is embodied carbon, the emissions released in extracting, manufacturing and transporting materials and in the act of construction itself. Cement production alone accounts for a substantial share of global carbon dioxide emissions, and a mid-rise concrete building may embody as much carbon before it opens as it will emit through decades of operation.

Once this is acknowledged, the arithmetic changes. A study of twelve commercial sites by researchers at a northern university estimated that demolishing a sound older building and replacing it with an efficient new one would take between 25 and 40 years to “repay” the carbon released during construction. Many of the towers now going up will not last much longer than that before they, too, are gutted or replaced.

There is a cultural argument as well, though it should not be overstated. The two- and three-storey shophouse, with its shaded arcade and its mix of shop below and home above, embodies a way of living that suited a hot climate long before air-conditioning. Its deep, narrow plan encourages cross-ventilation, and its arcade shelters pedestrians from both sun and rain. Not every old building merits preservation, and nostalgia is a poor basis for planning policy. But these structures represent accumulated knowledge about building for this climate, and we discard it at our peril.

Developers will reply that refurbishment is costly and unpredictable, that older structures rarely meet current fire and accessibility codes, and that the land is simply too valuable to leave under low-rise buildings. These objections deserve a hearing. Adapting an old building is often more complicated than starting from a cleared site, and some will need substantial structural work. Yet much of the difficulty stems from regulations written with new construction in mind, which treat every alteration as if it were a fresh project.

Policy could tilt the balance. Planning authorities might require developers seeking demolition permits to submit a whole-life carbon assessment comparing demolition with reuse. Building codes could include proportionate provisions for existing structures, permitting alternative ways of achieving equivalent safety. Tax incentives currently reserved for new energy-efficient buildings could be extended to deep retrofits.

None of this means freezing our cities in place. Cities must grow, and some sites will rightly be cleared. The point is that demolition should be the last resort, justified by evidence, rather than the default. The most sustainable building, as architects increasingly like to say, is frequently the one that already exists. It is time our planning system began to act as though it believed that.

passages.title: Making Results Travel: Witnesses, Instruments and Standards in Early Experimental Science
paragraphs: Modern readers tend to assume that a scientific result, once correctly obtained, is simply true, and that anyone with the right equipment could confirm it. Historians of science have spent the past half-century complicating this assumption. Their central insight is that, for much of the history of experimental inquiry, the hardest problem was not producing a result but persuading others, often hundreds of miles away, to accept it. A finding that could not leave the room in which it was produced was, in any practical sense, barely a finding at all. This article traces three strategies by which early experimenters sought to make their results travel: the cultivation of credible witnesses, the replication of instruments, and the eventual standardisation of measurement.

The first strategy was essentially social. In the experimental societies that emerged in Europe during the seventeenth century, an experiment was frequently performed before an audience whose members were expected to attest to what they had seen. Because few people could attend, however, experimenters also developed a distinctive style of writing, describing their procedures, failures and apparatus in such painstaking detail that readers might feel almost as if they had been present. Historians have called this technique “virtual witnessing”. Its effectiveness depended heavily on the standing of those involved: the testimony of a gentleman of independent means was widely presumed to be disinterested, whereas that of a paid assistant or craftsman, whose hands actually operated the equipment, was seldom recorded at all.

The limitations of this arrangement became apparent whenever a result was disputed. Detailed prose could convey what an experimenter claimed to have done, but it could not compel a sceptical reader to believe it. Opponents could, and did, argue that a description was incomplete, that the apparatus leaked, or that the witnesses were partial. Such accusations were difficult to answer from a distance, since a reader could neither inspect the apparatus nor question the witnesses directly. In such disputes, the only decisive move was to build the instrument oneself and see whether the result could be reproduced.

This proved far harder than the printed accounts implied. Early air pumps, telescopes and electrical machines were costly, temperamental and largely handmade, so that no two examples behaved in quite the same way. Surviving letters between experimenters in different cities record repeated failures to obtain effects that the original authors had described as straightforward. Some historians have argued that these failures reveal the importance of what has been termed “tacit knowledge”: skills such as knowing how tightly to seal a joint or how to judge whether glass is sufficiently clean, which practitioners possessed but could not fully articulate in writing. On this account, successful replication frequently required a person, not merely a text, to travel—an apprentice sent to learn at the original workshop, or a visitor who had watched the apparatus in use.

If skills could not be fully written down, quantities could, provided that everyone agreed on what the numbers meant. The third strategy, which gathered pace in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, was the standardisation of units and scales. Before this period, measurements of length, weight and temperature varied considerably from place to place, and even a careful report might be uninterpretable to a reader elsewhere. Temperature is an instructive example: dozens of thermometric scales were in circulation, each defined by different fixed points, and comparing readings across them required conversion tables of uncertain accuracy. The gradual adoption of shared scales, together with the creation of physical reference standards kept under controlled conditions, allowed results to be compared without anyone needing to travel at all.

The significance of this shift is difficult to overstate. Standardisation transformed trust from a matter of personal judgement into a property, as it were, of the measurement system itself. A reading taken with a properly calibrated instrument could, in principle, be checked against a common reference by anyone, regardless of social rank. Instead of asking who had performed an experiment, readers could increasingly ask how it had been performed and against which reference its instruments had been checked. Several historians have accordingly portrayed the rise of standards as a democratising force in science, one that diminished the weight of reputation in favour of procedure.

This interpretation, though attractive, has not gone unchallenged. Dr. Arunee Wongsakul, a historian who has studied the national measurement laboratories established in the late nineteenth century, points out that standards themselves had to be maintained, compared and certified by small groups of specialists, whose authority was no less social than that of the earlier gentleman witnesses. In her view, standardisation did not eliminate the need for trust so much as relocate it, from individuals to institutions. Moreover, access to calibrated instruments remained unevenly distributed, so that researchers in less wealthy regions often found their results discounted for want of the right certificates.

A further caution concerns how such histories are told. It is tempting to narrate the development of experimental credibility as a steady march towards objectivity, in which each stage corrected the shortcomings of the last. Historians have long warned against this kind of “Whig history”, which judges the past by the standards of the present and treats earlier practitioners as imperfect anticipations of ourselves. The three strategies described here did not simply replace one another; witnessing, replication and standardisation coexisted for long periods, and each persists in some form in laboratories today. The countersigning of a laboratory notebook by a colleague, for instance, is in effect a modern act of witnessing.

What, then, does this history suggest? Most fundamentally, it indicates that scientific facts become robust not merely by being discovered but by being made portable, through texts, people and shared standards, each of which depends on networks of trust. This need not lead to the relativist conclusion that scientific knowledge is nothing more than social agreement; an air pump either evacuated its chamber or it did not. It does, however, suggest that the reliability of science is an achievement that must be continually sustained, rather than a property that results possess automatically.

passages.title: Care at a Distance: Migration and the Changing Obligations of Adult Children
paragraphs: Across much of Asia, the obligation of adult children to care for their ageing parents has long been regarded not only as a moral duty but as the foundation of social security. In societies where public pensions are modest and residential care is scarce or stigmatised, it is typically a son or, more often in practice, a daughter or daughter-in-law who provides daily assistance as parents grow frail. Large-scale labour migration, both from rural to urban areas and across national borders, has placed this arrangement under considerable strain. When the children who are expected to provide care live hundreds or thousands of kilometres away, how is the obligation fulfilled, and by whom?

Early research on this question tended to adopt what might be called a deficit perspective. Studies conducted in the 1990s and early 2000s frequently described the parents of migrants as “left behind”, a phrase implying abandonment, and documented the loneliness, unmet health needs and economic insecurity that some older people experienced after their children departed. A related body of work introduced the concept of “global care chains” to describe how women from poorer countries migrate to care for children and older people in wealthier ones, while the care needs of their own families are met, if at all, by relatives or by still poorer paid workers. The resulting image was one of care being extracted from the global South and transferred to the North, leaving a “care deficit” behind.

This perspective drew attention to genuine inequalities, and its insights remain valuable. Over the past fifteen years, however, a second generation of research has questioned whether physical distance necessarily implies the absence of care. Drawing on extended fieldwork with transnational families, scholars have proposed that care be understood not as a single activity requiring physical proximity but as a bundle of distinct practices: financial support, practical assistance, emotional support and the provision of accommodation. Migrants, they argue, may withdraw from some of these practices while intensifying others.

Financial support is the most obvious example. Remittances, the money migrants send home, frequently pay for medical treatment, home improvements and the wages of local helpers, and in some cases they enable parents to enjoy a standard of living that would otherwise be unattainable. A 2023 survey of 1,600 older adults in four provinces of northeastern Thailand, for instance, found that those with at least one child working abroad were more likely than those without to have sought treatment for a chronic condition in the preceding year, a difference the authors attributed largely to remittances. Nonetheless, money cannot easily substitute for help with bathing, dressing or getting to a clinic, and the same survey found no difference between the two groups in reported loneliness.

Emotional support, meanwhile, has been transformed by communication technology. Inexpensive smartphones and video-calling applications now allow many migrants to see and speak with their parents daily. Researchers have described the resulting sense of being together despite separation as “co-presence”, and have documented how migrants use it to monitor parents' health, remind them to take medication and participate in family decisions from afar. Some older people report that frequent video calls make them feel closer to a distant child than to children living in the same village. Yet the benefits are uneven: parents with poor eyesight, limited literacy or unreliable connections may be excluded, and the expectation of constant availability can itself become a source of strain for migrants working long hours.

Perhaps the most important contribution of the newer research is its attention to how care is redistributed within families and communities. When one child migrates, care responsibilities rarely disappear; rather, they are renegotiated. A sibling who remains nearby may assume most of the practical work, sometimes in exchange for a larger share of remittances or of a future inheritance. Neighbours, temple networks and village health volunteers may also fill gaps. The concept of “care circulation” has been proposed to capture these reciprocal, shifting flows of support across generations and distances over the life course, including periods when migrants return home to provide intensive care themselves.

Not all scholars are persuaded by this more optimistic account. Critics contend that, by emphasising migrants' ingenuity and the resilience of families, the newer literature risks romanticising arrangements that rest on the unpaid labour of those who stay behind, most of whom are women. The sister who stays to look after a parent, they point out, often does so at the cost of her own earnings and education, and her contribution is easily rendered invisible when researchers focus on the migrant. Others caution that studies relying on interviews with families who have maintained close ties may overlook households where relationships have broken down entirely, thereby overstating how well care survives migration.

These criticisms suggest that neither perspective is adequate on its own. Migration does not simply abolish care, but neither does it leave care unchanged. Its effects appear to depend on factors such as the number of siblings, the gender of the migrant, the availability of local services and the size of the economic gains that migration brings. An older parent with several children, one of whom migrates and sends regular remittances to a sibling who remains, may be well supported; a widow whose only daughter works abroad on a short-term contract may not.

For policymakers, the implications are twofold. First, ageing and migration policy can no longer be designed in isolation from each other; countries that depend on labour emigration need to invest in community-based care services that do not presuppose a co-resident child. Second, the hidden contribution of family members who remain should be recognised, whether through carer allowances, flexible employment protections or respite services. Filial obligation is unlikely to disappear in the region, but the forms through which it is expressed are changing, and public institutions will need to change with them.

options: Labour migration has led most ageing parents in Asia to be abandoned by their children.
Migration reshapes, rather than simply removes, the care adult children give their parents, with uneven results.
Communication technology has solved the problems of caring for parents from a distance.
Remittances are the most valuable form of care that migrant children can provide.

care by daughters-in-law has declined in recent decades
although sons may be expected to provide care, women usually do so

carefully chosen from a larger group
obtained by threats or force
quoted from a longer piece of writing

questions.q: What is the function of paragraph 3?
options: It provides statistical evidence for the deficit perspective.
It explains why the concept of global care chains was abandoned.
It acknowledges the value of earlier work before introducing an alternative view.
It summarises the policy recommendations made later in the passage.

questions.q: According to paragraph 3, the newer research treats care as
options: a single activity that requires family members to live close together
a mainly financial relationship between children and their parents
a duty that migrants abandon as soon as they leave home
a set of separate practices, some of which can be carried out from afar

to point out the limits of what remittances can achieve
to suggest that older people with children abroad were less lonely
to question the accuracy of the survey's other findings

live with one of the migrant's siblings

employ local helpers for bathing and dressing

refuse to help unless the migrant returns home permanently
rely entirely on temple networks and health volunteers
be paid a carer allowance by the government

pays too much attention to women who stay at home
underestimates the costs borne by family members who stay behind
relies too heavily on large-scale statistical surveys

dismissive of both as politically motivated

balanced, drawing on both while treating neither as complete
